utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Case number IT-95-14/2-T, the Prosecutor versus Dario Kordic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, your client is not here today. The position, as we understand it and we were told last night, is that he has sustained an injury to his leg playing football and has had to go to the hospital this morning as a result. The matter was raised with me yesterday evening, and I gave him permission to go. It seemed the obvious and sensible course to follow. On the other hand, although he's not here today, it would seem sensible at least to get on with what we can. What I have in mind is that the rest of the cross-examination of this witness is completed by Mr. Kovacic and any re-examination is completed. We'll then review the position and see if he's back or not before we begin with the next witness. There is also one other point: If he's not back and we have time to spare, there are the procedural matters to continue with, which at some stage have got to be dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge. Let me respond, if I may. I gather the guards noticed what our client had told us about; that is, he had been injured substantially in a soccer game. His leg apparently is substantially swollen. The guards, on their own initiative, reported it up the chain to the registrar, and it was thought appropriate to take Mr. Kordic to the physician today. I'm told that he -- the guards think he will be back by 10.15. That being the case, perhaps much of what I'm saying is moot. To the extent that he's not here, we except to the -- it should be "except," not "accept" -- [Realtime transcript read in error "accept"] to Your Honour's ruling that the trial go on in his absence but acknowledge that there will be minimal harm because this is Mr. Cerkez's examination, and Mr. Kovacic will continue. Should we have to go into testimony beyond that, like the next witness, then I think we need to readdress the lack of Mr. Kordic's presence. I should stop there. As to procedural measures, there are some minor things we can deal with. We still do not have, relative to the dossiers, the summary prepared by the Prosecutor of the investigator, which would be critical to our position on the dossier, so I think we're not ready to do that. Mr. Smith should be here for that as well. We'll prepare for that as early as tomorrow or Thursday, hopefully, but there are some other minor matters we certainly could clear up should Mr. Kordic not be present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll go on, and when Mr. Kordic gets back, he can be brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: If I may, Judge May, could I take up two very minor housekeeping matters. There was an exhibit yesterday, I believe it was D35/1, that needed an amendment, and I told you I would have that amendment, and I have it here.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: And I just have a slight clarification to the position that I articulated to the Court yesterday when asked what the Defence's position was with respect to the telephone call between Mr. Kaknjo and Mr. Kordic on the night of October the 19th. That's contained at page 3758, lines 18 to 25, and page 3759, lines 1 to 2, of the transcript. I just want it to be absolutely clear as to what the Defence position is, and it's this. Mr. Kordic told Mr. Kaknjo that political negotiations to resolve the conflict in Novi Travnik would only be possible if commander Refik Lendo would cease hostilities and acknowledge responsibility for attacking HVO forces in Novi Travnik. Mr. Kaknjo's position was that he did not have the authority to make this commitment on the part of the Muslim forces. I just wanted that to be clear. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll go on with the cross-examination. Mr. Kajmovic, I'm sorry you've been kept waiting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Kovacic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kajmovic. Let us proceed, please. Yesterday we left off at Mr. Budimir. You mentioned him as one of the moderate Croats in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My question to you is very brief, if you would just tell me about two or three additional persons from the Croatian Community in Vitez who are frequently mentioned. Mr. Ivica Santic, was he a legally elected official in the elections in 1990?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He remained active in the social and political life throughout '92 and '93?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that generally speaking, the SDA leadership judged Santic to be a constructive person?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: For the most part, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in a way, it was considered that political forces within Vitez -- in other words, local political forces -- are endeavouring to maintain, quote unquote, normal relations, regardless of the general trends within Bosnia and Herzegovina outside of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were such attempts. At least, the Bosniak side always tried to maintain decent relations within the community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we say that within the Vitez municipality, the relationships between the two populations, or between the two parties, if you will, in this attempt to maintain good relations, that they were better -- these relations were better than outside of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were attempts to make it work.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since you mentioned these attempts, my further question to you is regarding Mr. Josip Silic.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he another important person in this community?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time when you talked about joining the defence forces, is it true that he proposed a compromise solution to establish HMVO? In other words, Croat/Muslim Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were several attempts to establish both a local government and to unify military forces.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So was Silic one of the persons who played a positive role?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, you could say that he was one of the moderates. But just a moment, can I just give a bit of clarification, when you talk about moderates and nonmoderates?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps not, because we did not go into that that far. Let me just move on, please. Mr. Pero Skopljak: Just in general, would you define him as a radical or a moderate?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was absolutely a radical.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean in the beginning of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Throughout.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean including '93?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. In your diary, in certain places, you obviously noted down, at certain meetings, certain notes. This is obviously subject to interpretation, but let me quote you a couple of excerpts from the evidentiary material that were discovered to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: These are the notes of today's witness. I'm going to quote it in English, and yesterday the witness confirmed that these were the notes which he had turned over to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your first note on Mr. Skopljak is from a meeting on 17 February --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think the witness really ought to have these notes in front of him, if they're going to be read not only out to us but also translated from the original to English. I think they ought to be--

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: May I explain, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The suggestion of my dear colleague, Mr. Nice, is, unfortunately, practically impossible because the corpus of the original notes -- and I can show it to you -- are in very, very bad condition; and what is the worst is that the so-called ERN number is hardly visible on some pages. On a majority of pages, one cannot see that. Translation is by those here in numbers related to the Croatian text, and whenever I was trying to find, after reading in English, where is that in Croatian language, I was not successful. Besides, I will not read more than one sentence or two sentences in, I think, only two places. So, however, if the witness has any doubt, we can later on leave the notes with him and he can probably give us. I don't know, otherwise we will lose five hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If you read the portions out to the witness and see whether he accepts that that was what was in the notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It gives the RN number. I can simply make the sheet available immediately and it can be seen by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (interpretation) Great, even better.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let's begin.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first excerpt where you mention Mr. Pero Skopljak was at page 00328319. This was according to the notes, so that's my reservation. This was a meeting on 17 February in Travnik. You mentioned that this was a joint meeting of three municipalities held in Travnik. It is the maintaining of peace. Then you mentioned people who were present. There was Kaknjo, then Pero, then Marijan Skopljak, and then "P. Skopljak", and I assume that now that is Pero Skopljak. Then Kaknjo and so on. Then on the following page, next to the name of Pero Skopljak, you say as follows: "The parties and not the military," in other words, not the military bodies, "should control." In other words, they should run policies. Then you say, "We have a single enemy, the Chetniks." Then you say, "No decision should be taken without the agreement of both sides. Both ethnic groups should have say over the economy," and so on. Do these notes refer to Mr. Skopljak and his discussion in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me show you another excerpt. This is page number 00328424. Sorry, 25 is the last two digits.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) For everybody else who is looking at the English text, it is on page 95 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, you mentioned a meeting of two ethnic groups held on 28 May 1993. Again obviously several participants attended, and this is their discussions, and then at the top of page 96 of the English version, which is the bottom of the same page in Croatian, another note of yours, and I assume this refers again to the discussion of Pero Skopljak. I'm going to read to you starting from the middle of those notes, and I assume that the Prosecutor will have found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I hope I've found it, but as Mr. Kovacic says, no, the RN numbers don't appear, but I hope this is the right page. I've counted them forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, could you please look to see whether that is the right page? This should be somewhere at the bottom of the page, and the first note is about Santic. This is still the meeting of 28 May '93. Then you have a note, several phrases on Pero.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I see "Santic" towards the bottom, and then up at the top, "Smajo Djuzo". But up at the top, it's not a very good copy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, that is exactly my problem which I encountered when I tried to follow it in Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, I see "Pero" on this page.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see on this page that this is a meeting of the two ethnic groups on the 28th of May?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Up at the top, I see "'93", but I cannot see the rest. But it is possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like you to make as much of an effort as you can. Perhaps you may not need the note.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: That is exactly the problem we were facing which I told you at the beginning. I was a couple of hours and was not able to recognise in Croatian. (Interpretation).

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, would you just leave that aside for a second, and I hope that you will just agree with me on the text that I read you. Somewhere midway through this discussion regarding Pero, we come to the following sentence, and this looks to be a quote from his. "Even though it was said of me that I was the brains behind the radical strain of the HVO, I personally have problems with extremists who accuse me of being pro-Muslim. I am not that way, and I am trying to be democratic. I have no personal --", and then I cannot read the rest of that sentence. I'm skipping two pages now, and again you quote Pero, and he says as follows: "In my opinion, a military coup was committed in the entire Bosnia. It refers to all three ethnic groups, and the civilian authorities are practically without any influence. We should proceed to some sort of militarisation and create a strong police force which will be organised on the ethnic basis among the populations. The suspicions between the groups, which some consider necessary, I believe that common people will be able to detach itself from," something in that sense. Am I refreshing your memory?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this true or not, that Pero Skopljak, at least in this period, did not have his own political views but rather that he joined these moderates? Do you think that this is true or not? I think it would be sufficient if you just say so.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If this continues like that, if I'm just asked to say "Yes" or "No", then I don't know where I'm going. You're just not allowing me to explain certain processes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Explain what it is that you want to say.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: First I want to say that I had turned over one notebook to the Prosecution, and the other notebooks, which probably the Defence has, are the notebooks which were left behind in my house and after the occupation of Vitez, and perhaps there was an additional notebook which was left behind in the logistics base in Vitez. After the occupation of town, the HVO probably took possession of these notes. So this is not a diary. These were just notes taken down at particular meetings. It was my duty to report to my staff after certain meetings and to attend to give summaries of discussions of participants in these meetings. However, I feel compelled to clarify something regarding Mr. Santic and Pero Skopljak. These were two really intelligent persons, unlike Ante Valenta who somehow expressed his views very openly. Unlike him, Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak were much more careful about this. In meetings, they would say one thing, but in practice, other things were done. I could give you examples of such behaviour of Pero's. Let me give you one example where his actions totally mismatched his words. He was always very careful in meetings. For instance, once in the crisis staff, we agreed that the joint police would not wear any types of markings, any types of insignia, because we could not agree on them. The meeting went on for five hours. The next morning, after it had been concluded that the police would wear no insignia, Pero Skopljak arrived in a uniform with the HVO insignia. In other words, his action was totally counter to the words. So I had to take down what he had said in the meeting and so it isn't quite true, but in practice you have a totally different behaviour. I can also mention to you Pero's statement when we went to meet with Serbs in Tolovici and there were some problems with Bosniaks and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I mean the witness is now going on to another subject, Tolovici, which is another village. I will have some questions about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: I would like to add something. (Interpretation) Mr. Kovacic, as you are going to proceed with the cross-examination of the witness, you should also allow him to answer, of course, sometimes by "Yes" or "No" to confirm that which you put to him. But, as he has just done, you should also allow him to compare these notes and the practice. I do not think we can talk only about notes, such as they are. It is said that these are notes which were taken immediately after a meeting and so that one could really know what the meeting was about, and I think we really need a better and more accurate idea about the situation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Judge Bennouna, of course I could not agree more, but here we are dealing with bits and pieces of information which can be gleaned from the notes of the witness, and as the Prosecution said at the beginning of the case, this case is based on a number of indications, or a circumstantial case as it is usually called in common-law countries. We therefore have no way out but to try to get, to glean, to obtain the opinion or to realise what was the opinion of the witness on the basis of those odds and ends of notes, of information. As for the witness's allegations, I believe we clarified yesterday that the Defence has -- and these quotations that we address here all come from the diary or -- yes, rather notes, to be more accurate, which the Defence was given by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution obtained them from the witness himself. We have no other notes, nor did we intend showing to the witness some other notes, the ones that he's referring to which may have come into the possession of the HVO. To conclude, let me round off this set of questions. My question was simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You gave us an additional explanation, and will you please tell me only "Yes" or "No" as to whether my conclusion is correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know what is your conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. I was just warning you.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, give me a conclusion and then I'll tell you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So according to you, Pero Skopljak did not change his political option throughout the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We could have finished with this straightaway a long time ago before, if you had said "Yes" or "No". Now, let us move on to Slimena, and with reference to the operation of the crisis staff, you mentioned both in your statement -- at some point you said that the attack on Slimena was conducted by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'll ask a few questions about that. You were a member of the crisis staff?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In April and May 1992, the crisis staff sat three or four times a week; "Yes" or "No"?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So it was very efficient?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, in terms of the number of meetings, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Will you please confirm whether the following members were members of the crisis staff; Ivica Santic, Fuad Kakjno?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Hakija Cengic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sefkija Djidic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There was a change. There were some changes subsequently in the army command. There were some changes, and I don't think --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it during a period of --

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Perhaps towards the end, because there were some changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Marijan Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe he was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Munib Kajmovic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Stipo Krizanac?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These people, and Croats and Muslims were about 50/50, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The crisis staff composition was such that people came in individual capacities, that is, they did not join the crisis staff as individuals but as persons representing individual branches of activity?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all these people held some positions, important positions, across the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among other things, the crisis staff decided to issue a threat and, if need be, attack Slimena or, rather, the JNA depot in order to get the weapons of the Territorial Defence which the army had formerly taken from the municipalities; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was talk about how this could be recovered, seized, or taken or what.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But can we say that the decision was taken and that these weapons were taken?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not remember that a final decision was taken, a definitive decision was taken, but there was a discussion, that is true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Do you remember if, during that discussion, the preparation of the decision or the decision itself, whether there was even mention of a man who would conduct the military action to this effect?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is quite possible that this was discussed, that this was raised, even though I do not remember. But it just may be that the name of Filip Filipovic came up.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Was perhaps Cerkez mentioned alongside Filip Filipovic as his deputy or assistant?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot really remember that we went into all that detail.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was perhaps the time set or was it left to Filipovic, as a military man, to plan it and do it?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that various dates were mentioned, but in all likelihood it was decided that Filip Filipovic should do it at a time seen as best for him, because it wasn't entirely about Vitez, it was also the weapons for Travnik and Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Is it correct that the Territorial Defence or, rather, the BH army provided Bofors and a three-barrelled 20-millimetre gun provided for the purpose? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know about it because I really did not deal with military matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. But in reports about this military action, did you learn that the Bofors crew of five members which participated in that action, that three of them were Bosniaks of that crew?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, I did hear some rumours that it was possible that some members of the BH army took part in that, but I have no idea. I received no information whether they came from Travnik, from Novi Travnik or from Vitez, so that I really do not know. What I do know is that Filip Filipovic was in charge of that action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I should like to remind you that one of the crew was Rajdzo Haskic who did come from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know that man personally, but I just don't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. If you don't remember, you don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned a meeting in Travnik which dealt with the distribution of the seized weapons and ordnance. Do you remember -- of course, there must have been plenty of discussions about this and a number of meetings, as far as I know. Do you remember whether that evening, at the site -- that is, at Slimena, in the depots -- that Mr. Sifet Sivro and Ramiz Dugalic had come to that place and talked to Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about that, but were Sifet Sivro and Ramiz Dugalic, were they commanders in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Sifet Sivro was a lower ranking commander in the army, and Ramiz Dugalic was with the staff in Vitez for a while, and he was responsible for security matters.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in those subsequent reports and various discussions which ensued, did you hear that several persons died at Slimena -- Muslims, Bosniaks, by and large -- after Slimena had been taken?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not know that, but I do know that two HVO members were killed. One came from Gornji Mosunj and the other one from Donji Mosunj, and I attended the funerals of both of them. But they were not killed in combat; they were killed during the attack on Slimena.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear something about casualties after the HVO had taken that compound?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I heard that other people had sustained injuries from mines, from landmines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear that an uncontrolled group of people, a large group of people, also tried to force their entry there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I spent about three hours in front of that depot, and I was watching all these things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, but I'm inquiring about the time. Was it at that time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, that was between 10.00 and 1.00.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean that evening when they took the depot?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, no, it was the next day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next day after?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, the depot was taken sometime in the morning on the 4th of May, and as of 10.00, half past 10.00 until about 3.00, we were in front of the depot, and we watched all those scenes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it then true -- but just "Yes" or "No" -- is it true that a sizable group of people tried to enter through minefields in the direction of the woods? I believe there were very many casualties.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because people went through there uncontrolled, and I don't know how many of them, but quite a number of them, yes, sustained injuries.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. And after that, when the weapons were taken out, they were all distributed. We can discuss [unintelligible] and so forth, but let us see, generally, who took the lion's share?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Well, it is difficult to say, really. As I said, in my view, those were four or five thousand men from three municipalities, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and Vitez, and people came both in an organised manner or disorganised manner, on foot, various vehicles, and so forth. They broke into that depot. They were taking out without any control whatsoever, so it is really difficult to make any estimate and say which side, whether it was the Bosniak or the Croat side which took a larger part of that. Of course, we did try to agree on their controlled distribution, but it was simply impossible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. So let us try to conclude: Is it a fact that both sides came by a certain number of weapons?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just one more detail, did anyone get some burnt weapons because there was a fire in the depot?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of scorched weapons, of damaged weapons, and people tried to repair them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But did you hear that such weapons, scorched weapons, turned up in Ahmici later on? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I do not really remember any detail, but there were those scorched weapons which people tried to repair, to mend, to make them -- to put them back to -- to use them again.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Now I should like to proceed to the blockade of Ahmici in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, may I just briefly comment, the questions which we have just covered? May I? These are very important. The crisis staff was mentioned here.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Under the decree of the presidency of B and H, in municipalities, pursuant to the legislation to the laws of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, no crisis staff could be set up, and it was the war presidency which was to be established in case of a crisis. That is, the war presidency of the municipal assembly, specifically, in Vitez, on the basis of rules strictly laid down so that the crisis staff was set up in contravention of the laws, because the HVO and HDZ structures would not comply with the law. So that is one of the facts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Before we proceed to the roadblock in October 1992, you mentioned one thing, and so you reminded me. Anto Valenta -- you mentioned him when we made mention of some important individuals -- was he ever a member of the municipal structures? Was he the favourite of municipal structures? As far as I remember, he was for a while the president of the HDZ in Vitez; that is, he was the president of the political party, so he wasn't elected to the municipal government at the elections?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But by and large, would you be more precise?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, he did not hold any, exactly, post in the municipality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Anto Valenta, just tell me whether -- "Yes" or "No" -- Anto Valenta was more engaged, in quotation marks, in big business, and did not really do anything at the municipal level; is that the correct impression?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it is not. He also had his hand in municipal affairs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Let us now move on to this roadblock. You said that the roadblock was set at two points on that road next to Stara Bila, so was it by the building company Bosna?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the second location was by the village of Ahmici -- that is, the Catholic cemetery -- at this S-curve?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, correct. It is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this road, tell me, please, insofar as the traffic is concerned, I can go from Bihac to Travnik using that road?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, you can't. You have to take a roundabout. But if you go from Bihac, then you go to Mrkonjic, to Jajce --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's microphone is switched off. We cannot hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt at this stage. Mr. Kovacic, the witness gave no evidence about the roadblock. The evidence which he gave was in relation to a telephone call after a meeting at the headquarters on the night of the 18th/19th of October. We've already had a great deal of evidence about the roadblock itself, and it's not going to assist the Trial Chamber to hear more. What, of course, you are entitled to deal with is the meeting at which it's said your client was present at the headquarters of the army in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Okay.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were several meetings on the 19th, particularly in the evening of the 19th October, at the time this roadblock was removed; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, it was removed the next morning, during the HVO attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, no, no. I don't mean it was lifted. I'm talking about when it was set up.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It was set up on the 18th in the evening or 19th the morning. I don't really know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. This is not all that relevant, but during the 19th, there were a number of meetings or several conversations, several contacts, in an attempt to find a solution, to remove -- to lift that roadblock?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is possible that the military held various meetings, but I don't know about them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many meetings did you attend, or how did you conduct any talks in this regard?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: On the 19th, in the evening, when Ivica Santic and Mario Cerkez came, that is the only time, the only occasion when I was present.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Dr. Mujezinovic mentioned a conversation on the same subject, on the 19th of October, in the evening hours. Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think that on several occasions, Sefkija Dzidic went to the health centre, invited by Franjo Tibolt, and he did conduct some talks with Mario Cerkez, and he should know the details, because I do not know any particulars about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Kajmovic, can we then agree that there were several contacts and several talks in these attempts to find a peaceful way to remove the roadblock?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, that has already been dealt with several times by you. Now, can we move on to the meeting at which the witness can give evidence, at which he said he was present?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please tell us another thing -- I'm moving on. In September and October, '92, Bosniaks and Croats fought together against Serbs and tried to keep Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, those were members of the BH army and HVO in Jajce.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And possibly some reinforcements for the troops in Jajce, did they go from Central Bosnia, did they use that particular road?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You again raise military matters and military things, and I really did not particularly know about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. I'll ask you now a few questions about -- you said in your earlier statements, and also in your evidence here before the Court, that the civil servants -- rather, municipal clerks -- had to sign a statement of their loyalty to the HVO; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the SDA, as a party, discuss it and take a view, take a stand on that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did it instruct Bosniaks how to do and what to do?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us, in just a couple of words, what did you advise Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I could do it in several sentences. I cannot do that in two words.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, will you please try to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At the time, the HDZ already had an unlawful government, an enforced government, and there are about 1.200 people employed in the municipal assembly; about 50 per cent of them are Bosniaks. On the basis of the decision of that government, they conducted a fictitious job distribution, or rather, nothing changed in practice, people still kept their jobs, but they had to sign this new distribution of jobs in order keep them. So basically it said the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, then at the end of this decision, it was signed by the HVO government. Practically, whoever signed that decision, he was pledging loyalty to an unlawful government, and those who would refuse to sign that statement, of course, could not keep their jobs. So the executive board of our party discussed the matter, and we concluded the following: People of Bosniak origin should sign that statement, because otherwise, if they were to be dismissed from their jobs, we simply could not support them and their families. And those executives who were elected in the elections, or appointed by the party, were told that they could not do that, regardless of whether they would lose their jobs or not, because, of course, it was easier for us to take care of two or three cases rather than 50-or-so cases.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Thank you very much. From what you have just said, Mr. Kajmovic, if I have understood you well, actually, all workers -- not just Bosniaks and Croats, but all the workers in the municipal organs of authority -- were given these new decisions on employment to sign, on a form which now had a different heading and a different signature. Was anything changed regarding labour rights and all rights emanating from employment?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with those details, but most probably not, but this was an absolutely illegal government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. You've explained that. My question is that these were symbols involved?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Symbols are the form, but the substance behind it is something else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Nevertheless, the Bosniaks continued to work in the municipal administration, with the exception of a few officials, as far as I understand it?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So no one threw them out?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A few words about the celebrations of the first anniversary of the BH army that you mentioned, in Stari Vitez, where you met Cerkez. Let me put the question to you. My first question, Mr. Kajmovic, is: Are you quite sure that the meeting was held on the 15th of April -- or rather the celebration -- on the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Will you repeat the date?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told me it was the 15th of April. Are you quite sure it was the 15th of April, 1993, the anniversary?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, it was an anniversary meeting held in Stari Vitez, in the centre. It could have been on the 14th as well, because we had two days of celebrations, actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You see, let me follow on to that by saying, according to other data, information, even some other witnesses, this was on the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were two days of celebrations, the 14th and the 15th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you said it was either the 14th or the 15th -- it really doesn't matter -- that Cerkez came to the celebration as well?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he come as a representative of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, as a representative of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was on good terms with his colleagues in the army, like Sefkija Dzidic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They had frequent contacts to deal with various problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The formal part of the celebration that Cerkez came to attend was held in the fire brigade centre, wasn't it, on the second floor?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that, you had something to eat and to drink, as is customary in our country? Where was this?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This could have been on the ground floor, because there was a cafe on the ground floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the ground floor level?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you stay there, or did you leave?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was there briefly, maybe for half an hour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was some kind of an interruption because there was an incident at the petrol station?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you sure that Cerkez went there, to the place of the incident?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that some representatives of the army went there too, and I think that he went.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you're not quite sure about that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I cannot claim that with certainty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear whether he came back, or maybe that he didn't go at all? Did you hear that he stayed there until quite late, talking with them and having dinner with them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. A few matters linked to your stay in Stari Vitez after the outbreak of the conflict on the 16th of April. You told us that a part of the Territorial Defence, or rather the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Stari Vitez, was relatively poorly equipped, and that apparently throughout that time you were surrounded; that is, until April 1994, until the Washington Agreements?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also told us there were several very strong attacks on Stari Vitez by the HVO. I would like to know, how did you manage to endure a year of siege? And from what we heard until now, you had no resupply of materiel or ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did some Bosniak forces manage to enter Stari Vitez and bring some ammunition and equipment with them?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, but I can explain how we managed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Does that mean that you had abundant stocks before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If you allow me, I will explain it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you know the Prosecutor will be asking you more questions after me, so you can explain then, but please allow me to continue with my questions. Maybe we can come back to that a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I should ask the Chamber for leave to show this sketch to the witness that I made, myself, the main points of the encirclement, because I have a few questions about this, and some other witnesses will be coming to testify about the same issues. With the help of the usher, may I distribute the sketch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, the only matter I raise is this: How relevant are the events of the siege for the matters that we are deciding?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, the relevance is that we hold that regarding the time after the outbreak of the conflict -- that is, as of the 16th of April, '93, onwards -- we claim that this was a civil war from then on, a war between two peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because the third people was not represented in this part of the country. And I should like to hear from the witness, who was present there, in the surrounded part of Stari Vitez, to see where their positions were. He told us that the HVO army was besieging Stari Vitez and that they were under siege, and the position from the indictment is that only one side was armed and was waging war, whereas the other side was unarmed and was not at war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And who do you allege started the civil war?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I'm not quite sure of that, nor is my client, as to who actually started the war. Another point, to which we will devote a considerable amount of time in this trial, Vitez has some specific characteristics regarding the pre-war period, and also the wartime period, in another sense. The conditions there were different than in other municipalities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, and we would like to show that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask questions, but would you have in mind the clock and the amount of time that's being taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D23/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, we shall try and be as brief as possible. I made this sketch myself to expedite things and to avoid unnecessary explanations, so this is a schematic presentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A little bit more down. Okay. Usher, could you please give one copy to the witness on the table so he can see better? No, there's only one. There is one more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, you have a copy in your hands, so let us go through it very briefly. In the middle is the main road going from Vitez towards the Catholic Church, going upwards. On the right-hand side, which is the north, about half a kilometre away is the Lasva River. To the left is this other road, with these prominent facilities: The stadium to the left of Stari Vitez, then the SPS factory further away from the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, the place that I have marked with the number "1," it is about the same level as the Nihad Omanovic house, near the utilities building? Was that the front line between the HVO and the army? Was that the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, roughly there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the opposite end, which I have marked with "2," that is Nikola Krizanac's house, or to the right we have the Mlakic houses. Was that the line of separation?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, right next to the rubbish dump.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Having mentioned the rubbish dump, was the BH army headquarters near there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, for a time, in a building in the area known as the rubbish dump.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the communications centre there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not sure. Possibly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's go on. To the north, on the right-hand side of this sketch, was the Lasva River, as a defence. To the left, near the stadium, is an exposed, low land, in the military sense?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the point marked with the number "3," that was the fire brigade centre that we spoke about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is where this jubilee was observed?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have also marked the municipality building which was controlled by the HVO. Just for the purpose of orientation, that is at the bottom of the sketch.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Is that number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The municipality building, on the bottom of the page. The municipality building we saw yesterday when the Prosecution gave us the pictures, set of the pictures. It is out of Stari Vitez. It is within the part of the city controlled by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, but is it number 6?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir. Yes. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And while we are dealing with it, there are some various other matters which are untranslated on this document. Above that, "Skopljak"; is there a reference to his house?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Which number, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Above "6."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, this building is marked as Skopljak house -- Skopljak, Ivo, I-V-O. This has nothing to do with the guys we are mentioning, Pero and Mario.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And then, above that, we have two buildings which don't seem to be referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Nida, N-I-D-A, Omanovic, O-M-A- --

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Nihad. Nihad Omanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: "Nihad." Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Also name of the house owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And above --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The one above that is a tire repair shop. V-U-L-K-A-N-I-Z-E-R. Vulkanizer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And on the other side of the road --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) The left side is a communal services base, Vitkom. That was the name of the company.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: And above that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mosque. Then above is fire-fighting base. Up on the top is Catholic Church.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, the BH army members that were in Stari Vitez held those front lines to defend themselves from potential attack by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And they were deployed in the way that the army command felt was best?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were platoons divided up into sectors?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were certain sectors territorially. How many soldiers there were in each sector it is difficult to tell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's fine. You told us as much as you knew. What about the platoon near the stadium? Was it led by Mr. Salih?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with those details, but I know that Salih was there somewhere.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Tatarevic? I don't know his name. He was next to the tyre repair shop, wasn't he? Didn't he lead a platoon there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, there was a Tataravic near the line towards the church up there, a policeman called Tataravic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind. That's not all that important. Did you have any prisoners of war in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, there was one, a man who was riding his bike, I think, and who came from the direction of the market and entered this part of Stari Vitez and was taken into custody. That's as much as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me refresh your memory. But first tell me, do you remember that there was a joint commission for the release of prisoners?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Frequently joint commissions were set up. Whether this particular one existed, again that comes within the military domain, but it's possible. Possibly, did exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I should like to tender the document. We have the translations too. Could the usher distribute this document? It is for everybody.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The document is marked D24/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The English translation is attached on the second page, and, Your Honour, it is a translation I did myself, because we located this document only a day ago. Of course, it could be checked by the registrar, later on by the translation unit, but I did it correctly. I can assure you of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It could be perhaps grammatically wrong. I apologise if it is. But not by the subject.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kajmovic, will you look at the signatures first so that we see the members of the commission, Hajdarevic Refik. He's a Muslim, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a Bosniak, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there is Borislav Jozic. He's a Croat, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then there's Stipo Krizanac, another Croat?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Nihad Omanovic. He's a Bosniak, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Regarding Nihad Omanovic, he was an intelligence officer in the command, wasn't he or in the staff?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: He was in the staff for the defence of Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And he was an intelligence officer, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Something like that. That is the kind of work he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document is dated the 16th of May. Would you agree with me that this commission functioned, as obviously it was composed of two members representing each side, and we conclude from this that three persons were released and they signed their release?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that is what is shown on this document.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know nothing about those persons, as to whether they were civilians or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know. I just know of this one person who was arrested who was not even armed. He just happened to drive by on his bicycle, and that is why I remember it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind. Let's leave that for the moment. Tell us, during the siege of Stari Vitez -- did UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I would just like clarification on the document you just tendered. The members of the joint commission, I take it, were Bosniaks and Croats. Who was on the commission as members there? Can you identify those?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The person under item 1 is a Muslim Bosniak. Under number 2 and 3 are Croats. I mean the numbers in the signature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: 2 and 3 are Croats. Number 4 is Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Of the persons who were released --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Judging by the names, all of them are Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kajmovic, judging by the names of the three released persons, would you say they were Croats?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is that all, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Let us go back to UNPROFOR and the International Red Cross which entered Vitez on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the period from the beginning of the conflict until the end, that is April of 1994, you said?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Which means that they must have had the permission and approval of the HVO to enter as they surrounded the area?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know whether such a procedure existed, but they did enter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have any personal experience regarding the organisation of reciprocal family visits between Vitez and Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was after the ceasation of hostilities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Wasn't it during the war?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I'm not aware of it during the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In view of your status as a party dignitary, the party discussed this sometime in the summer of 1993, which means during the siege Ivica Santic offered the possibility for civilians to leave, to be granted refugee status, and to go where they wanted. Do you remember anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were such proposals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this discussed at a meeting at which Santic proposed this to Mr. Sefkija Djidic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: We had some negotiations towards the end of June, beginning of July, in the UNPROFOR base in Bila. Whether this was raised at that meeting or another, but I know there were such proposals. I personally received messages to leave Stari Vitez through a liaison officer of the British Battalion, Mr. Perry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you didn't leave?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, there were some Croats in Stari Vitez as well?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, a few.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were some?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did any Croats get killed during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I cannot recall now, but I do know that some Croatian houses were razed to the ground by Croatian shells.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about any other causes?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There may have been verbal incidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does the name Zoran Vidovic mean anything to you, who was killed in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I don't know, and I doubt that that was possible.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Dragica Prkacin?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If they were killed, then they were probably killed from HVO fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were certain houses confiscated for defence needs in Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: What do you mean "destroyed"?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, confiscated, requisitioned.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: There were some cases of abandoned houses being used for defence needs, both Bosniak and possibly some Croat houses as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us that you were in the civil defence at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you under the obligation to work?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was on the front line, but I was also active in the civil defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there a work obligation for people at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that could be described as such.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But that was a legal obligation under the regulations taken over by you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For a year, Stari Vitez and Vitez was separated, was divided. Did the BH army open fire towards Vitez from Stari Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Only in self-defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did operate?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may explain --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I don't think that is necessary. We are fatiguing the Chamber with this conflict. But there was an exchange of fire?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Each time the HVO attacked, we had to defend ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember any light artillery weapons that you had there?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as I know, we had two or three 60-millimetre mortars, but they were not in use because we didn't have any shells, and a hand-held launcher, which as far as I remember was captured by HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any snipers?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I am not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was about Stari Vitez. Let me now ask you a few questions linked to some of the statements you made, as a point of clarification, more or less. First of all, in the introduction you told us that before the war in Bosnia, you were a teacher of history in school?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: May I take it then that you are familiar with programmes of study and curricula in Bosnia; at least you know them better than I do, the textbooks and things?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was familiar with the curricula for three-year studies and the four-year secondary school or grammar schools. Then there was the medical school which had a different programme of studies, but of course I am quite familiar with these.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But will you confirm as much as you know? What you don't know, you will tell us. There was a question raised here in connection with another matter. As to the plans of instruction in the Republic, and I'm talking about the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, we're talking of the period prior to April '92, were those same plans and programmes in effect when the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina acquired independence?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no time for any serious revisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So they remained in force for a certain period of time, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say the same of textbooks?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, because there was no time to publish new ones.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So now we became a sovereign new state. We are no longer a Socialist/Communist country. We're no longer a part of ex-Yugoslavia, but we used the textbooks we had?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, coupled with certain instructions received from educational institutions that certain subjects should be viewed from a slightly different angle and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we are now approaching the time for a break. Is that a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very much so, and I guess after the break I will need a maximum of 15, 20 minutes, not more than that, maximum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honours, a clarification, please. My Colleague Mikulicic, by following the transcript, pointed out that at page 35, line 2, you asked who had started the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, in other words, what is our theory. My understanding of it was that it referred to the conflict between Croats and Muslims, and my answer was that I did not know and that my client did not know. But talking at the level of the Vitez municipality and that portion of Central Bosnia, our submission is that the Muslim side was the one which started the conflict which then spread in '92 and '93. But we do not have any general knowledge, how the conflict between the HVO and the army, that is, the TO, had started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. May I continue?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation)

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, first let us just conclude the part on the education which I asked you about. When I referred you to your diary earlier today --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) May I ask the usher's assistance, please, to show the witness the document? For those who are using the English text, it's on page 20. We were able to identify the original page in the witness's notes. This was a meeting. I'm going to read it out loud to you in English. It may be very difficult for you to follow it. This is a meeting of 30 December '92. It looks like it is either a meeting of the party or some Bosniak body, and there are certain conclusions there. There are three that I'm going to read to you. Under item 2 -- number 1 is not relevant for this, but in number 2 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, let me ask you, was this a meeting of the party or some broader body? Can you define?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that this could be a party body.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I know that this is a terrible copy, but are you able to identify anything there? Then I'm going to read it out, the English version. Under 2, it says that the school is not going to be working on Saturday, that this day would be used for a rest of the teachers and pupils?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Oh, yes, under 2, stop the practice of having regular school classes on Saturdays and use this day for rest of the teachers and for their activities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And it says that all Bosniak children, that the language used should be called Bosnian language?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then, obviously, there was another point, that 20 per cent of salaries of Muslims should be -- every employed Muslim -- should be allocated for the support and assistance of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this is authentic?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Can I conclude, therefore, from this, and considering what problems you had, that the curricula was adjusted as you went along, and was this what the party was trying to do here?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe that my testimony would lose its meaning if I were not allowed to explain something. I need to point out that the Croatian side forced upon us the Croatian dialect, and then this came as a response to that. So we asked that the Bosniak children be told that their language was Bosnian. In other words, what is done here is you're avoiding mentioning the cause of what this discussion was about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me ask you something else. What was the language, or official language, in Bosnia, until '94?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The official language was Serbo-Croatian or Croat-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a Bosniak language?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Not officially.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there an ethnic group in the former Yugoslavia which was called Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Since the'70s.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But this was to denote an ethnic group, not a religious group?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, this was done at first, and then it was also done to denote both.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the Muslims, unfortunately, had no official language at the time?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: But they were at first not recognised as an ethnic group, either, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But what was the language that they spoke?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The language of Serbo-Croatian or Croat-Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kovacic, what's the relevance of all this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Two things, Mr. President. One, that a couple of days ago we had a document which was tendered into evidence, I think it regarded Vares, where the local HDZ was prescribing the official language for schools. What I'm trying to point out was that everybody was doing it, and it was logical, because everybody had sort of inherited the curricula and textbooks from the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which is their enemy now. So it is a natural reaction. I don't know if the Serbs did it, too. Perhaps not, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This assertion is not correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. Kajmovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, let us move on now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've seen enough of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, could you tell me, do you know of any case where a Bosniak or a Croat, from the territory of Vitez municipality or surroundings, had come back from the war in Croatia, where he may have been at the time, and joined in the war effort -- in other words, joined military forces, joining any arm, the HVO or the Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: At this moment, I could not recall any particular names, but I know that a number of people had gone to the front line in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we agree that when the war in Bosnia started, that there were people who came back home?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Very probably they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there such people on the Bosniak side?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, there were some people on the Bosniak side who had gone to Croatia to try to defend it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know of cases when, once the war in Bosnia started, the people started coming back home?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was not following these instances, but I'm fairly sure that there were some.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
