utterances.text: (Interpretation) May I ask the usher to pull the -- I think it's exhibit number Z2154. It's a map, a statistical chart or map. Can I also ask for assistance -- it was introduced as D82 -- sorry, 8/2.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, this was produced by you?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me just review it. This is the area of the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The full lines which cut through this area, and again I -- it's an accurate rendering of the map? One is to the north, one is to the south. It denotes the demographic boundary?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. This is the line that denotes the separation -- that is, the military separation -- between the HVO and the BH army. But it's somehow remained an administrative boundary to date.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. So to the north, only the -- in the northern and southern section, there are Muslims, and in the central area, which sort of coincides with a valley, that's where the Croats are?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But I do not see Serbs anywhere here.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to the census information which you provided, there were some Serbs there, and from what I know, they were for the most part concentrated in the north: Hrasnica, Ljubici, Grabak, Trnovlje Tolovici, Zvizda, in these villages?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Can we please have the witness be given map 8/2. Can you perhaps locate these villages? They can be seen on this map. Mr. Usher, could you please place it on the ELMO? Could you please give the witness a pointer, or a magic marker, perhaps blue, colour blue?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness, would you please show at the map -- could you please mark these Serb villages in blue.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Tolovici, Hrasnica, there were some there; Grbe, Trnovlje. It's very close, further up and to the right. Here we are. Yes, Trnovlje. Yes, Grabak, Hrasnica, Tolovici, Ljubic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Clearly they are to the north, in the northern section, and we saw the census figures. Do you recall, there was quite a bit of a political debate, at the political level, at the party level, in '91 and the early '92 when the Muslims from these villages who were a minority there pushed the Serbs out?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: With the Court's permission, I cannot just stay silent over some things that the Defence is doing. There were 1.051 -- 1.501 persons were Serbian. In the village of Tolovici there was a larger concentration, about 250 Serbs, in addition to about 150 Muslims. Most of the Serbs lived in the town of Vitez, and then in the area near Kruscica. So your avoiding certain facts leads to wrong conclusions, and I would not want to speak anything but the truth here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let me rephrase this. Were there still Serbs in these villages at the end of '92?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: They voluntarily moved out of the Vitez municipality, prompted by the SDS party.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kovacic, could the Chamber, could the court know exactly what are you driving at here with your questions, sir, because why do we need these statistics? These statistics, we have accepted them as estimates of the witness, and where do you want to arrive at? You have been at this cross-examination for almost two hours, yet we said yesterday it would last more than one, and instead of -- but if we are going now into a demographic analysis, I'm afraid this is going to take us too far, particularly in comparison with the testimony of this witness so far. So will you please try to be more precise and more concise as well, because this cross-examination really is now taking more time than it was volunteered properly for the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) I am just trying to point out that it has certain other implications. The approach of the Muslim side to the weakest ethnic group in the Vitez municipality, which practically disappeared from Vitez by the end of '92, and this was the beginning of ethnic conflict in the area. So I believe that this is a relevant fact.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: It is not a relevant fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) It is relevant, because the line of separation remained such throughout the conflict, and it had been established in 1992, so we clearly see that the Vitez valley which was controlled by the HVO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Ask your question, please. Ask a question directly. You do not really have to go into all this demographic structure. This is not the subject of the testimony. Ask your question directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Very well. Sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, in late 1992, were there Serbs still in this area which we just described?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, until about October 1992, when mass exodus started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following October?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: In October and November they moved out and they turned over their weapons to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Could you now tell me, looking at the map, this line of separation, these two full black lines, in practical terms, was this the active line of separation between Croats and Bosniaks in the Lasva River Valley and the Vitez municipality throughout 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is the final line of separation up to 25 February, 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was it the same when the conflict started?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From 16 April, 1993, when the conflict broke out, until 25 February '94, it only experienced minor changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So these were lines established in the beginning?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, these were lines established in the very beginning and with minor changes remained such until the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you will agree with me, and you can just say "Yes" or "No," some portions of that line had already been established in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, absolutely, this is absolutely untrue. This line has nothing do with it. It is only that the town of Vitez was already occupied on 20 October, 1992, when the last member of the BH army was driven out of the town and so you could only say that the town had been occupied then.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Looking at your map or chart, you only show the area of Vitez municipality. What was to the east and what was to the west of this municipality?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: You can see here that to the east is the municipality of Busovaca. To the west is the municipality of Novi Travnik and partially Travnik and to the north is the municipality of Zenica and to the south partially it's Busovaca and the municipality of Fojnica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, the Muslims are directly linked to the areas to the north, which is Zenica, where there was the Muslim municipality, and then the Croats in Busovaca, was linked to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, that was a partial result of the occupation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then to the south it's again Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: This is a mountainous region so it is practically uninhabited.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is then leaning on another municipality which was controlled by the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Kajmovic, thank you for your effort, notwithstanding all the problems. Your Honours, I have concluded my examination of this witness. Maybe just one additional question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said earlier that about 75 per cent of the territory of Vitez municipality was controlled by the BH army and about 25 per cent by the HVO. Is that reflected in this chart?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, there's a question that you asked at the beginning of your cross-examination as to the citizenship of the witness or witnesses. Can you just explain for me the particular significance of the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. President, the import of this should be sort of one of the elements of crime, of a criminal offence, which must exist, and it's related to internees and has to do with the vocabulary in protocol 2. The term used there, if I'm correct, the term used there is "protected persons", and it seems to me, that is, in our view, and we already referred to that at a pre-trial brief, that it is untenable, it is unacceptable -- no, let me rephrase it. If it is an international conflict, then they must be citizens of two different countries, which does not hold true of an internal conflict. So that is our thesis. We are preparing, well, a kind of expert testimony. Of course, it is a legal matter, but we should like to call an expert on citizenship. In the former Yugoslav state, the citizen doctrine was quite advanced and specific, in my humble opinion, as of 1945, in all the legislation as of 1945, and especially in the constitution of 1954.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just a few matters, please, Mr. Kajmovic. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few matters, Mr. Kajmovic. Re-examined by Mr. Nice:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, the Muslim parade and its similarity or dissimilarity from the Croat parade of which you've spoken, to what extent was the Muslim parade similar or dissimilar?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the Bosniak side, there was also an oath-taking procedure, that is, a common procedure in all democratic countries, so that members of the BH army took the oath of allegiance, saying that they would be defending the sovereignty and integrity of the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in contrast with the Croat side, who also took an oath of allegiance in which they had to pronounce an oath which said that they would be defending only Herceg-Bosna. So these are two completely different things. Secondly, the HVO kept this review, this parade -- there was about five or six hundred combatants, and I forget where they took this oath, and which was a show of force, practically, to intimidate the Bosniak population. So whereas the army worked in neighbourhood communities, they did it at the town stadium, which was open to everyone. Everybody could come, and through the wording of this oath of allegiance at the same time meant a threat to the population of Bosniak origin, so that is the difference.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The answer, as it reads on the transcript, is arguably a little ambiguous, so I'll just clarify it. This probably can be dealt with very shortly. Are you saying that the oath by those at the Muslim or Bosniak ceremony constituted in any way a threat to others or not?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next topic, the telephone conversation involving Fuad Kakjno. Just a couple of questions on the versions that have been outlined by the Defence. Do you accept that Kaknjo was said to have no relevant authority by Kordic in this phone call?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just an objection to the form of that question. It's very ambiguous, Your Honour. I believe that we had represented to the Court that it's the Defence's position that Mr. Kaknjo told Mr. Kordic that he didn't have any authority to take positions or to make decisions on behalf of the Muslim military forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I misread my note. Quite right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As to that proposition, do you accept that?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: The substance, the gist of it, is not whether somebody had the authority or not. The important thing is the Bosniak side did its utmost to prevent conflicts or at least to bring them to an end, the ones that started. So if any negotiations took place on the cease-fire, Kaknjo could negotiate and sign such agreements, such understandings, and his signature would not be contested by anyone on the Bosniak side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Mr. Nice, I think you have to word properly your question. We are not really interested in the opinion of the witness but what he heard being said by Kordic himself, by the accused. So we are not really seeking the view of the witness, and will you please try to direct the witness in this direction. "What did Kordic say to Mr. Kaknjo with regard to Mr. Kaknjo's authority?"

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, you've heard the Judge's observation, and the question that you were answering in the form of the observation by Mr. Sayers was that Mr. Kaknjo told Mr. Kordic he didn't have any authority to take positions or make decisions on behalf of the Muslim military forces. Do you accept that proposition, that is to say, did Mr. Kaknjo say that, or not?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Dario Kordic conditioned all the negotiations on this [indiscernible] and the army. He was the one who was putting the terms by this fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One other question on this topic. You were asked to consider Mr. Fuad Kakjno's evidence on an earlier occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I have transcripts if the Court needs to see it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One question that you were asked was this: "The only thing is," you were asked, "he didn't add the curse that was heard as Kordic was approaching the telephone?" You were not asked to deal with the earlier statement that Fuad Kakjno had made to investigators, and for completeness, that should be before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I simply provide the relevant two pages of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I object to that, Your Honour. That's beyond the scope of our cross-examination. We didn't ask any questions at all about Mr. Fuad Kakjno's statement, just about his sworn testimony in the Aleksovski case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He was asked about the testimony. It must be relevant to put in his statement too. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I just hand in -- it's got the cover sheet, for identification purposes, and just two of the pages of the statement itself. Can I propose that it becomes 2154,3? If the English version could be placed on the ELMO first at the next sheet, please, Mr. Usher. It will be page 5 and it picks it up, and I can deal with it quite quickly, although the Court can read it, I have no doubt, more swiftly to itself than I can read it out. But it's the paragraph that starts at the foot of page 5, "On the 19th of October," and it then goes over the page, and I needn't set out this person's account in detail for these purposes. At the top of page 6, "Santic told me he had already talked with Kordic and Kordic wouldn't listen to him. Santic told me if I wanted to talk to Kordic, I could, and he gave me a telephone number for Kordic." I remember I've omitted to give copies to the interpreters. I apologise. They've got it in front of them. "There was a suggestion that myself and Santic go to Novi Travnik and try to settle it. Santic said that, 'If Kordic agrees to listen to you, I will go to Travnik with you and try to reach an agreement.' When Santic gave me the telephone number, I could see that it was in Novi Travnik. I called Dario Kordic. Someone answered the phone, and I asked him if Dario was there. I didn't introduce myself when I told the person I wanted to talk to Kordic. The person said that Dario was there but busy at the moment. I heard sounds of Kordic talking to someone giving orders. Kordic sounded nervous and began swearing. Kordic then said, 'What is going on with Vitez? We have to do it with Vitez.' Kordic then picked up the phone and asked who it was. I identified myself and told him that I had talked to Santic." Then it goes on and deals with the phone call.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, is this witness going to give evidence in this trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If he is available to us and willing to come. That may not be the position, and I'm not sure at the moment. But it seemed, in light of the possibility that he may not, that it was appropriate to complete the prior accounts he gave.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, I've read out the passage from a statement of Mr. Kaknjo. I don't invite you to comment unless you say that anything he says in it is untrue to your recollection. Is there any part of that that you say is untrue or with which you disagree? That's the limit of my question.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No, there isn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The next topic, and there are only about three more in all and the others are short, the next topic concerns questions that were asked of you about the blockade at Ahmici, and again the Court will recall, probably, the cross-examination yesterday. I have hard copies available, if that would be helpful, but the question with which I was concerned was Mr. Sayers' cross-examination where he was pressing on the witness that the witness was acknowledging that the blockade was introduced at a point in the road of particular military or strategic significance, and he was quoting his testimony to him, and at one stage he said this: He said, "Once again, on page 5733, your testimony in Blaskic, quote: 'So this was one of the motives, to take control of this road communications, and this would be the purely military aspect of it.' Did you state that in the Blaskic case, one and a quarter years ago," to which the witness said,"No, no, please, don't do that. I do not agree, absolutely not. The order was to put up the barricade, to halt, to prevent the passage of units to Novi Travnik." In light of that difference between the witness and Mr. Sayers, who went on to say that was the evidence in the case, can I just provide the evidence and put it in its context again? This can become --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Do you have the page number, Your Honour? I can't find that in the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 5372 and 5373 in the transcript in Blaskic, and may it become 2154,2? This can similarly be placed on the ELMO to begin with on -- because it's double-side copied, to begin with on the front side, first sheet.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, did the questions about the blockade arise at the end of your examination in Blaskic and in answer to questions from Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I believe it is somewhere towards the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kajmovic, just wait there, please, and listen to what's going to come, and there may be a short question at the end of it. The Court will see, on page 5372, that Judge Riad was asking questions in relation to the witness's research project of which he had spoken and whether he considered genocide was used as a means of ethnic cleansing in Vitez. In his answer, the witness says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There is an objection. Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not an objection, Your Honour. I was extremely confused when I heard the page numbers. It's actually page 5732 and 5733, not 5372.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My mistake. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: A slip of the tongue, no doubt.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Indiscernible] cross-examined for it yesterday. It goes on, "In my thesis, I touch on the genocide in Ahmici. I did research this issue and I identified the exact number of victims there," over the page, "and I tried to ascertain the reasons why this was done and why in Ahmici. And apart from general motives, there was some local or practical reasons as well. One of the practical reasons for this genocide was that the local commune, where there were 508 Bosniaks, was on the road Vitez-Busovaca. It was a strategically-important point, and only at this point was there any danger that it could be cut off and that the HVO may not be able to use it for military purposes. So this was one of the motives, to take control of this road communications," and I'm afraid my copy now misses the next two words, but I can find it rapidly. "This would be the purely military aspect of it." You then went on to say, Mr. Kajmovic, "But there is another aspect why genocide was committed there. One was the motivation which was revenge, and on the 18th of October, 1992, when the HVO attacked Novi Travnik on the orders of the Commander Hadzihasanovic of the 3rd Corps, a roadblock or barricade was put up in Ahmici. It was attacked by the HVO and it was removed within about one hour of gunfire." Then you go on to deal with one young man being called, and you said, "So this barricade briefly slowed down the HVO troops' movements from Busovaca," and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So when the passage of evidence, and this is the only question that I want you to deal with, was put to you, which as the Court will see, the passage that begins with the fresh paragraph on 5733, when the passage of evidence was put to you about the motives being to take control of road communications, were you referring, at the time you gave that evidence, to what had happened earlier or to what had happened in April of 1993?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: If I may answer some three questions here --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I only want you to answer the one question. Namely, when you gave that passage that Mr. Sayers put to you in detail, were you -- it may be self-evident from the transcript, but were you speaking of what had happened in October of 1992 or what was happening in April of '93?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I was referring to what had happened in October 1992. Here one needs to distinguish between the terms "strategically" and "literally relevant". This is a term in the open conflict, that is, as of the 16th of April, '93, when the fighting began until the end of it. Then a point, an elevation or whatever, may be important, more or less, strategically important for the military. However, things that happened in October '92, the army wanted to stop -- to prevent the movement of HVO units because of the strategy they were using. Since they were better militarily organised, better equipped also, they were using the tactic of attacking one municipality after the other, and after taking one, then going after another one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you, because it's helpful to have the Chamber have your answer precisely to the question that's asked, and I think you gave that answer. The remaining topics are very short, I think. First, reference to a grenade that may have or did kill some children in the course of the conflict. Just "Yes" or "No", if this is possible. Did that come from Stari Vitez or not, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: No. Nor was that possible even in theory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Because?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: (Interpretation) Your Honour, I should like to object. Two or three times the witness, both during the examination-in-chief and cross, he said that he was not a military expert, that he knew nothing about military matters. Now, just a moment ago, he gave us some information about military strategy, and now he has all of a sudden become a ballistics expert, an expert on shells.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, he is not. The witness is entitled to say what he knows happened. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it possible? You say, "Not in theory." Just explain why.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: From the place where a shell killed several children of Croat ethnicity to the house where I lived, until the HVO attack on the 16th of April, there are no more than 50 metres from there to the line in Stari Vitez, that is, the front line which was to the south and southeast. From that place to our line, there is about a distance of some 200 metres or so. There are some private facilities there and so on and so forth. And I really, as a layman, tried to reason, and I wonder how can one direct a shell at those 200 metres of such a calibre when we know that in Vitez, there was simply not a weapon of that calibre, of that size? I mean I know what the ground looks like physically. These distances are very short there, and --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's the answer. You were asked about the restocking by Stari Vitez of food and so on in the course of the conflict. You said you could add to it. I want you to do so in just two or three sentences, please. Was it necessary to restock food and other items in the course of the conflict or were there adequate stores?

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: I think that the Defence referred to stocks of ammunition and not food, but I can reply as regards both items.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Can I?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: As far as food was concerned, through the Merhamet charitable society some food had been obtained, some 20 tons of flour, which was stored in Stari Vitez. Thanks to that flour, about 1.200 inhabitants managed to survive until the so-called White Road Convoy, as it was called, when we received a certain quantity. Then the population had some stocks in reserve in their own households so that the population did relatively well as regards food because there was sufficient quantities of flour. As for ammunition, as I was on the front line and had a rifle, on average we had 50 to 60 bullets. We didn't have more than that. In a period of less than one year on the front line, where I kept regular duty, I fired 10 to 15 bullets in all. So considering the amount of ammunition used, I could have remained there for another three years because the orders were that we were not allowed to fire a shot except in extreme necessity, and that meant if an HVO soldier reached our very trenches and dugouts, in which case we had no other choice. So that is the explanation, and I may add that some 40 or 45 out of the 60 I had were left at the end.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was something you wanted to add briefly in the cross-examination by Mr. Kovacic about the use of the term "moderate" as opposed to "radical". If, on reflection, there's nothing you wish to add, don't feel you have to provide an answer. If there's something you want to say, try and put it succinctly so that it can help the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. There was some debate over Pero Skopljak and the town mayor, Ivica Santic. Some of the Croatian officials, political officials, at certain meetings, especially when differences of view existed between us, they would tend to make certain statements that were not fully in control. Some of them, like Ivica Santic and Pero Skopljak, were very careful in choosing their words, and their statements and actual activities in practice on the ground were quite different. My intention was to mention this because the Defence, quoting my notes which I was obliged to convey to members of the executive board of my party, that is, the minutes of those meetings, so I took note of those statements, but I can also mention different statements made which give a completely different characterisation of Pero Skopljak as a radical. I could mention a meeting held in the village of Tolovici, to which we were invite by Serb representatives, for us to hold a joint meeting in an elementary school there. Myself and Pero Skopljak went to that meeting, and we tried to calm down the situation, to avoid incidents. Upon returning in his own car, passing through Krizancevo Selo, in conversation, I said, "You really did deliver a nice speech to the Serbs, which rather surprised me." His answer, and I quote him verbatim, if I may quote his words, which contain a swear word, he said that -- he cursed his mother: "They should be told one thing at meetings, while in fact every effort should be made to kill them." Of course I didn't take note of such things, because these were notes about meetings. But the impressions of all people there were that Pero Skopljak was an extremist.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the topic of your notebooks, you've spoken of other notebooks that may have landed up in other hands. We are not remotely interested in rumour or speculation.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Only if you have any evidence to point to where your other notebooks may now be, will you tell us about it? If you have no such evidence, we will move on to the next and last topic.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: My house is in the part of Vitez which is under the administrative control of the HVO, and after the 16th of April, my house was looted. They searched it and raided everything, including the notebooks in that house, so that probably those notebooks ended up in the hands of the HVO, be it the political, military, or police bodies of the HVO. That is the most probable conclusion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, it's been suggested that in the area of Vitez, the conflict was started by the Muslims -- again, this is not an opportunity for a long answer, and you don't have to give any answer at all unless you feel you can do so by reference to events -- but are you able to point to any particular circumstance or events that would assist the Chamber with who it was who started the conflict in Vitez? So have the question in mind, understand it, take a second or so to think about it, and then answer if you think you can point to particular circumstances or events.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: Yes. On the 15th of April, at about 4.00 in the afternoon, 16.00 hours, we had a meeting in Stari Vitez at which representatives of the Bosniaks were present, representatives of the army, the police, and the SDA party. At that meeting we analysed the situation in Vitez municipality at the time, and some people, specifically Kaknjo Fuad, Zeko Fuad, asked representatives of the army and of the police to tell them clearly what the security situation was. In fact, he asked the commander of -- Dzidic Sefkija whether he could sleep at peace. He asked Saban Mahmutovic, the police commander -- that is, the commander of the Bosniak section of the police -- whether they could sleep peacefully. Their assessments were that the situation was tense, but no different from what it had been the previous days. So we can now say with absolute certainty that their assessment was completely wrong, and had that assessment been better, probably the Bosniak side would have done something to defend themselves better. As this assessment was wrong, the next day, in the morning, at 5.30 a.m., the attack was launched, and even guards or guard duty that was held both by the army and the HVO, on the side of the Bosniaks, after midnight, the guards went back home to sleep; and the guards in Stari Vitez, in which the Bosniaks have a majority, the HVO passed through those guard posts and set light to the first row of houses near the stadium. Also, from the direction of the church, they reached the crossroads, where the road branches off to the so-called garbage dump, where a number of Bosniak houses were burnt and a number of Bosniaks killed, so that because of such a poor evaluation --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think I'm going to stop you there. Unless there's anything qualitatively different, any different type of event at about the same time that you want to turn to, I think I have enough by way of an answer.

utterances.speaker: MUNIB KAJMOVIC (Resumed)
utterances.text: All I can add is that the aggression was carried out by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Those are the questions I wish to ask of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kajmovic, thank you for coming again to the International Tribunal to give your evidence. You are now released, free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we turn to the next witness, the position of the defendant Dario Kordic should probably be reviewed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The position is this, as reported: That Mr. Kordic has been detained in the hospital for x-rays. At least, that was what was reported to the Trial Chamber. He won't be available today, but he will be tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Your Honour, one of the possibilities discussed amongst ourselves -- realising this problem now exists, and in order to take advantage of the one hour and 45 minutes in the afternoon remaining to us -- is, if it's technically feasible, to tape the proceedings, both video and audio, in a language the accused understands, Croatian. And further, there was access to, at the detention centre, a player, that he can review all of the afternoon's activities, in time, given their schedule of events and meals and whatnot, then theoretically he can review what has been done and what has been said. Now, apparently there is some dissent on that, so I'm trying to work this out. If you can give us a little time -- you agree?

utterances.speaker: MR. NAUMOVSKI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Okay. Apparently there's no dissent, but the mechanics of it are the problem, and I don't know the answers to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we don't know the answer to that. We'll have to find out. There's another ten minutes, quarter of an hour, before the luncheon adjournment. Are there some matters we can deal with during that time?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Probably comparatively few free-standing administrative matters. There is the question of the protection of the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I actually want to establish one further thing with him. I have been seeing him myself. There is one further thing I want to establish with him before I make the application, and I need an interpreter to do that. Before I sit down, the statement to accompany the dossier is probably, I think, in final shape now. Its earlier format was not what I desired the Chamber to have, and it had to be reformatted, and it's being considered by the witness. I'm not sure when he will be in a position, having checked it, to sign it -- I hope this afternoon -- but one way or another, it should be available to the Court and my friends this afternoon, but I don't think it can be available much before. I took the decision this morning, first thing, to cancel the remaining three witnesses who were flying in today because I could see, both from the time taken in cross-examination and from the potential problems of the defendant's ill health, that it was almost inevitable we wouldn't get through the witnesses who were present here and three more, however short those other three would be. But that, nevertheless, leaves us with a number of witnesses to be called, if at all possible, this week. On top of that, and I just remind everyone, the two witnesses who took the statement from Dr. Mujezinovic, and who have been the subject of complaint by the Defence, are witnesses I intend effectively to tender so that their allegations can be raised with them, given the importance they attach to those allegations. With the various movements of investigators from this building, it's sometimes better to make sure you have your investigators when they're available, because they may not then be available for some time to come. And it would be desirable, if possible, to deal with that issue -- which may not take very long -- this week as well. But that all suggests a rather heavy diet, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Just to give something else on which to chew, apparently, according to co-counsel, the detention centre, when you hand over a tape, requires it be 48 hours in advance, to review it, check it for security purposes. The suggestion I proffered earlier will only work if Mr. Kordic can review the matter tonight, because he, as you know from watching, is very active in the participation of his Defence, writes us notes all the time, and I perceive that if he had an opportunity this evening to read and review the tape, we could be up to speed. I make this proposal only for this afternoon. Cross-examination would be a far different thing in terms of our presentation of the next witness. We're trying to be as accommodating as we can, given his situation. I'm told tomorrow he will be with us, with his leg elevated, and I'm just taking it session by session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, inquiries will have to be made as to whether the suggestion -- which certainly is in a cooperative spirit, but whether in fact it can be followed through. It would seem that if the tape came from the Tribunal itself, a Trial Chamber, it would be difficult for that to be objected to, but bureaucracy works, sometimes, in a way which is unexpected.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: The logic of it is unassailable. I can cite to a case from my jurisdiction in which logic did not prevail, Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But we don't, clearly, want -- if at all possible -- to waste this afternoon. The fact that the investigator's statement is not available clearly hampers a discussion, but there may be matters which we can usefully discuss if we can't hear the evidence. We should certainly hear the application for measures, and any other housekeeping matters that we could deal with. If Mr. Smith can be available, so much the better, and if we can hear what submissions there are.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it may be, even if the investigator hasn't signed the document, a draft statement can be provided to show the general form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, anything of that sort. Half past 2.00, then. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.55 p.m. --- 24 25

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we left matters to be determined by the Registry as to whether it's possible to carry out what's been suggested. I don't know if you've been kept informed of what is feasible and what isn't, whether the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Stein, actually, is better informed on this than I because he's been making the enquires. He's told me the results of his enquires.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: As I understand, Judge, the good news is there can be an audio cassette made that the accused can listen to. We don't have yet the second prong of the issue, whether at the detention centre there is an audio cassette available with a headset that he can use to listen to the tape. Apparently -- have I got that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you like to speak, just --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is an audio cassette available, and they will take appropriate measures, if it's necessary that he should hear the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Because he has no machine to listen to it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: But there are machines in the detention unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEIN
utterances.text: Being technically challenged in all these things, I -- apparently there's no ability to do the video and audio that we have because it would require a real-time sifting out of all the various languages that come into the real-time video. So in order to see the witness as well as hear the witness, it would require some extra work on the part of the crew here to do just that, and the time required is literally the same time as the time of the tape. I think that's correct. So therefore we're left with just an audio or, alternatively, some intervention on the part of the Court to order a transcript made of the video consistent with the audio. Now, I suppose there's a third possibility, and that is that Mr. Kordic could listen to the audio and look at the video, although the two would not be in sync. So he would have his video recorder and his audio recorder and bit and piece together things, which is not necessarily a bad result. That's option 1 available to Your Honour. We'll do whatever you wish. Again, limited to the direct examination, not the cross, because our cross will be, in large measure, shaped by our clients' instructions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course. (Trial Chamber confers)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. If that's a possibility, we'll do that. It may be that the amount of evidence will have to be limited from the point of view of the practicality of the thing. Certainly, no more than an hour, because the accused has got to listen to it tonight.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That would hold things up, but it might be sensible, if we can get an hour's evidence in, to do it while we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm very happy to do that, and I think I have four witnesses here still for the week, many of whom have given evidence once or twice before; not many, some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The sooner we get on with it, the better.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we go into either closed, or if its sufficient, private session to deal with the issue of the protection of the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. But may I say that while we're dealing with it, whoever is taking this witness should aim to compress the evidence in chief into an hour. It really would save a great deal of time for everybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm sure I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's a substantial witness, I have no doubt, but still.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It may help if we simply go into -- I'm in the Court's hands, whether it's safer to go into full private session for the application to be made. I don't -- full closed session. I beg your pardon. While that's being done, the Court should have, as my friends opposite have, a summary in, on this occasion, seven pages. (Closed session)
